title: Watchfulness
hook: the first rung: simply paying attention to how you live

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: Mesillat Yesharim. Your line was the path of the just. Which familiar good thing did you do on purpose? Today, the bottom rung of Luzzatto's ladder. Day one thousand two hundred eighty.

Some evenings the drive home simply disappears. Keys in the door, coat on the hook, and no memory of a single traffic light. The body made every turn. Nobody was watching. Plenty of days go that way too: answered, eaten, scrolled, slept, with the person living them somewhere else. Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto put a remedy for that on the very bottom rung of his ladder. Before zeal, before purity, before holiness, the first trait he asks for is the one that makes the others possible. Today's word.
screen: `THE DRIVE HOME DISAPPEARS.` → `NOBODY WAS WATCHING.` → `THE BOTTOM RUNG.`

segments.voice: Zehirut. Watchfulness. Turn it four ways. First, what it is. In Mesillat Yesharim, watchfulness means a person looks carefully at their own deeds and ways: is this good, is this not, where is this heading? Not a mood. A habit of checking. Second, Luzzatto's picture of life without it. Someone who goes through life without watching, he says, is like a blind man walking along the bank of a river. The danger is real and close, and he doesn't see it. Nothing has gone wrong yet. That's exactly what makes the riverbank frightening. Third, why people skip it. Luzzatto doesn't blame laziness first. He blames the rush. The busyness of daily life presses so hard, he says, that people never get a quiet moment to look at where they're going. He reaches for a line from Jeremiah about a horse charging headlong into battle, too fast to see what's in front of it. A person can be good-hearted and still be that horse. Fourth, the Tanakh's own short version. The prophet Haggai, speaking to people busy with their own houses while the Temple lay unbuilt, says it twice: "Consider your ways." Watchfulness is that sentence turned into a daily practice. Some Mussar teachers pair it with heshbon hanefesh, an accounting of the soul at day's end, but zehirut starts earlier: in the middle of the day, in the middle of the drive, catching yourself while it's happening. It isn't about suspicion of yourself. It's about being present for your own life, so that the rest of the ladder has someone standing on it.
screen: `LOOK AT YOUR OWN DEEDS AND WAYS.` · `A BLIND MAN ON A RIVERBANK.` · `A HORSE RUSHING INTO BATTLE.` · `CONSIDER YOUR WAYS.` · then, large: `BE WATCHFUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch yourself for an hour. The sit is for setting it up. Settle, and breathe. Choose one hour later today. The commute, the afternoon at your desk, the evening with the kids. Picture it beginning. Now decide what you'll watch for. Not everything. One thing. How you speak when you're tired. What your hands reach for when you're bored. Whether you're actually listening. Rehearse the moment of noticing: a small inner glance, a quiet "there I am." No judging, no fixing; only seeing. Then let the picture go and simply notice yourself breathing right now. That's watchfulness, already starting. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for open eyes. The bell holds the time.
Zehirut. Watchfulness: paying careful attention to how you live. The first rung of Luzzatto's ladder in Mesillat Yesharim. Today's word.
Your line: be watchful. Today, for the hour you chose, watch for your one thing, and catch yourself at least once, gently. Day one thousand two hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Mussar students begin Mesillat Yesharim with zehirut, watchfulness, often practicing it by pausing during the day to notice their own actions, alongside a nightly accounting of the soul.

fork.setup: you're Luzzatto, explaining why good people fail to watch their lives. what do you point to first?
options: the rush of daily life leaves no time to look.
fork.reveal: he describes people pressed by busyness, like a horse rushing headlong into battle, with no quiet moment to look.

original.note: Hebrew: watchfulness, care; the first trait in Mesillat Yesharim.

trapdoor: what you thought: watchful means keeping an eye on other people.
what it means: looking carefully at your own deeds and ways while you live them.
what a scholar hears: Luzzatto pictures life without it as a blind man on a riverbank and blames the rush, citing Jeremiah's charging horse.

notes: Mesillat Yesharim ch. 2 paraphrased: watchfulness defined as examining one's deeds and ways; the blind man on the riverbank image; the pressure of daily busyness; the citation of Jeremiah 8:6 (horse rushing into battle). Confirm these are in chapter 2 (some may be in chapter 3) and fairly paraphrased.

Haggai 1:5 and 1:7 both contain 'Consider your ways' in JPS 1917 ('Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways'); 'says it twice' is based on those two verses. Confirm. The lesson does not claim Luzzatto cites Haggai.
Heshbon hanefesh is mentioned as a pairing Mussar teachers 'often' make; it was the subject of day 1254. Confirm 'often' is acceptable.
Practice: the outline asks to watch yourself for an hour; with a two-minute sit, the sit is used to choose and rehearse the hour.

Editor: Haggai's audience was misdescribed as 'people rebuilding their lives'; now 'busy with their own houses while the Temple lay unbuilt' (Haggai 1:4, 1:9), which also fits Luzzatto's point about busyness. 'Mussar teachers often pair' softened to 'some'; smoothed one practice line.
